questions.question: Gorbachev launched perestroika and glasnost in the 1980s to save the Soviet system. What did they do instead?
options: Restored growth but at the cost of political freedom
Opened criticism the state could no longer contain
Strengthened the Party by removing corrupt officials
Triggered a military coup that succeeded in 1989
questions.answer: Opened criticism the state could no longer contain
questions.explanation: Perestroika restructured the economy and glasnost relaxed censorship, and the second undid the first. Once people could publicly discuss shortages, Chernobyl, Stalin's purges and the Afghan war, the legitimacy of the system eroded faster than reform could stabilise it. Nationalist movements in the Baltics and Caucasus used the new openness immediately. A hardline coup attempt in August 1991 failed and accelerated the collapse rather than preventing it.
questions.memory_hook: Perestroika restructured the economy, glasnost relaxed censorship, and the second destroyed the first. Once people could openly discuss Chernobyl, the purges and Afghanistan, the system lost legitimacy faster than reform could fix anything. The 1991 hardline coup failed and sped up the end.

questions.question: Lexington and Concord in April 1775 began the American Revolution. What were the British troops actually sent to do?
options: Arrest John Hancock and Samuel Adams in Boston
Seize colonial weapons and powder stored at Concord
Occupy Concord permanently as a garrison town
Enforce the tax on tea at the Charlestown docks
questions.answer: Seize colonial weapons and powder stored at Concord
questions.explanation: General Gage sent roughly 700 regulars to confiscate a militia arms cache. Riders including Paul Revere spread word ahead of them, so militia were waiting. Eight died at Lexington in a confused exchange nobody planned. The British reached Concord, found little, and were harried for twenty miles back to Boston by militia firing from cover, losing around 270 men. Emerson's phrase came in a poem written 61 years later.
questions.memory_hook: Gage sent 700 regulars to grab a militia arms cache at Concord. Revere and others got ahead of them so militia were waiting. Eight died at Lexington in an exchange nobody intended. The British found nothing and were shot at for twenty miles on the way back, losing 270. Emerson's phrase came 61 years later.

questions.question: The Colosseum held around 50,000 spectators. How did Romans manage the crowds?
options: Numbered tickets directing each person to a specific arch
Spectators queued from dawn on a first-come basis
Only citizens with property qualifications could attend
Seating was auctioned before each day's programme
questions.answer: Numbered tickets directing each person to a specific arch
questions.explanation: Spectators received pottery shards marked with a section, row and seat, and eighty numbered entrance arches meant the building could reportedly fill or empty in about fifteen minutes. Modern stadiums use the same logic. Seating was strictly stratified by class, with senators at the front and women and the poor at the top. A retractable awning called the velarium, worked by sailors, shaded the crowd.
questions.memory_hook: You got a pottery shard marked with your section, row and seat, and eighty numbered arches meant it could empty in about fifteen minutes. Stadiums still work this way. Seating was rigidly by class, senators at the front, women and the poor at the top. Sailors operated the retractable sun awning.

questions.question: The US beat the Soviets 4-3 in 1980, but that was not the gold medal game. What did the Americans still have to do?
options: Beat Finland two days later, which they nearly failed to do
Beat Canada in a one-game playoff to decide the gold medal
Win a rematch against the Soviet team the following week
Survive a formal protest the Soviets filed over the result
questions.answer: Beat Finland two days later, which they nearly failed to do
questions.explanation: The Soviet game was a medal-round match, not the final. Had the US lost to Finland they would have finished fourth with no medal at all. They trailed 2-1 going into the third period before scoring three times to win 4-2. Al Michaels's do-you-believe-in-miracles call belongs to the Soviet game, which is why most people assume that was the final. The team's average age was 21.
questions.memory_hook: The Soviet game was the medal round, not the final. Lose to Finland and they finish fourth with nothing. They were down 2-1 in the third and scored three. Al Michaels's miracles call was from the Soviet game, which is why everyone thinks that was the final.

questions.question: The Olympic rings use five colours plus a white background. Why those particular colours?
options: They were the only inks available to the 1913 printer
Each represents one of the five original Olympic sports
They match the five colours of the ancient Greek games
Every national flag then contained at least one of them
questions.answer: Every national flag then contained at least one of them
questions.explanation: Coubertin chose blue, yellow, black, green and red on white specifically because every competing nation's flag contained at least one, so no country was excluded and none privileged. The five rings represent the inhabited continents, but no individual ring is assigned to a particular continent, despite persistent claims otherwise. He designed the flag in 1913 and it first flew at Antwerp in 1920.
questions.memory_hook: Coubertin picked those five plus white because every national flag then contained at least one, so nobody was left out. The rings mean the five inhabited continents, but no specific ring belongs to a specific continent, whatever people tell you. Designed 1913, first flown at Antwerp 1920.

questions.question: Tupac Shakur released only a few albums before dying in 1996. What has happened since?
options: His unreleased recordings were destroyed in a 2008 fire
More albums have been released posthumously than in his life
His family blocked all posthumous releases until 2020
His entire catalogue was withdrawn by his estate
questions.answer: More albums have been released posthumously than in his life
questions.explanation: Tupac recorded prolifically, reportedly finishing several songs in a night, and left a large vault. Seven posthumous studio albums have appeared against four released while alive. He also studied acting and ballet at the Baltimore School for the Arts, where Jada Pinkett was a classmate. He was shot in Las Vegas in September 1996 at twenty-five, six months before Biggie, and no one was ever convicted.
questions.memory_hook: He recorded fast, sometimes several finished songs a night, and left a huge vault. Seven albums have come out since his death against four while alive. He studied acting and ballet in Baltimore alongside Jada Pinkett. Shot in Las Vegas at twenty-five; nobody was ever convicted.

questions.question: The Star Wars cantina band plays music that sounds oddly familiar. What was John Williams told to write?
options: A score using only instruments invented for the film
Deliberately unpleasant noise to unsettle the audience
Something aliens might make if they heard 1930s swing
Traditional music from a real culture, unmodified
questions.answer: Something aliens might make if they heard 1930s swing
questions.explanation: Lucas asked Williams to imagine creatures who had picked up a Benny Goodman broadcast and tried to reproduce it with no cultural context, which is why the piece sits between swing and something slightly wrong. It is credited in-universe to Figrin D'an and the Modal Nodes. Williams composed the rest of the score in a deliberately old-fashioned late-Romantic idiom at a time when film scores had largely moved to synthesisers and pop.
questions.memory_hook: Lucas told Williams to imagine aliens who had caught a Benny Goodman broadcast and tried to copy it without understanding it, which is why it sounds like swing that has gone slightly wrong. The rest of the score was deliberately old-fashioned symphonic writing when everyone else had gone synth.

questions.question: The Beatles played their last public performance on a London rooftop in January 1969. How did it end?
options: Lennon walked off mid-song and never came back up
Police arrived after noise complaints and shut it down
They finished the planned set and walked off calmly
Rain forced them to stop after only four songs
questions.answer: Police arrived after noise complaints and shut it down
questions.explanation: They played about 42 minutes on the Apple Corps roof at Savile Row before police responded to complaints from nearby businesses. Lennon closed with a line about hoping they had passed the audition. The footage went into Let It Be, and the band split within months. Billy Preston played keyboards, and Ringo reportedly wore his wife's red raincoat because it was freezing.
questions.memory_hook: About 42 minutes on the Apple Corps roof before police turned up over noise complaints from the neighbours. Lennon signed off hoping they had passed the audition. They split within months. Ringo wore his wife's red raincoat because it was freezing.

questions.question: The Irish Sea separates Britain and Ireland. What lies beneath it that connects them?
options: An active fault line still pulling the islands apart
The world's longest undersea rail tunnel
A land bridge that existed until around 14,000 years ago
A freshwater aquifer shared by both countries
questions.answer: A land bridge that existed until around 14,000 years ago
questions.explanation: Lower sea levels during the last glaciation left Britain connected to Ireland and to continental Europe across Doggerland, now submerged under the North Sea. Ireland separated first, which is the leading explanation for why it has notably fewer native mammal and reptile species, snakes among them. Britain became an island around 8,000 years ago. Fishing trawlers still pull up mammoth bones and Mesolithic tools from Doggerland.
questions.memory_hook: Lower sea levels left Britain joined to Ireland and to Europe across Doggerland. Ireland was cut off first, which is why it has fewer native mammals and no snakes, rather than anything to do with Patrick. Britain became an island about 8,000 years ago, and trawlers still dredge up mammoth bones.

questions.question: Ribosomes assemble proteins inside cells. What makes them unusual among cell structures?
options: They can leave the cell entirely and function on their own
They exist only in animal cells and never in plant cells
They are the only cell structure carrying their own DNA
They are built from RNA, not protein, and act as enzymes
questions.answer: They are built from RNA, not protein, and act as enzymes
questions.explanation: The catalytic core of a ribosome is RNA doing the chemistry, not protein, which makes it a ribozyme. That matters because it supports the RNA world hypothesis: RNA can both store information and catalyse reactions, so it could plausibly have preceded both DNA and proteins. Ribosomes are also nearly identical across all life, which is strong evidence for a single common ancestor, and many antibiotics work by jamming bacterial ribosomes specifically.
questions.memory_hook: The part that does the chemistry is RNA, not protein, making it a ribozyme. That is a pillar of the RNA world hypothesis, since RNA can both store information and catalyse. Ribosomes look nearly the same in all life, which points to one common ancestor, and antibiotics work by jamming bacterial ones.

questions.question: The Dolomites look unlike the rest of the Alps, glowing pink at sunset. Why?
options: Iron oxide staining left by retreating glaciers
A rare lichen coats the summits above 2,000 metres
Volcanic ash deposits colour the exposed rock faces
They are fossilised coral reefs from a tropical sea
questions.answer: They are fossilised coral reefs from a tropical sea
questions.explanation: The range is built from dolomite rock formed as coral reefs and lagoon sediments in a warm shallow sea over 200 million years ago, then lifted as Africa collided with Europe. Fossil shells and coral are visible at 3,000 metres. The pale mineral reflects low-angle light with a pink and orange cast, called the enrosadira locally. The rock was identified by geologist Déodat de Dolomieu, who gave both mineral and mountains their name.
questions.memory_hook: They are fossil coral reefs from a warm shallow sea 200 million years ago, shoved up when Africa hit Europe, so there are shells at 3,000 metres. The pale rock catches low sun pink, which locals call the enrosadira. Named for the geologist Déodat de Dolomieu.

questions.question: What are phototropism and geotropism in plants — how do plants respond to light and gravity?
options: Phototropism = food storage; geotropism = immune response
Phototropism = growth toward light; geotropism = growth in response to gravity
Phototropism = reproduction; geotropism = nutrient absorption
Phototropism = chemical response to light; geotropism = growth toward water
questions.answer: Phototropism = growth toward light; geotropism = growth in response to gravity
questions.explanation: Phototropism is the growth of a plant toward (positive phototropism) or away from (negative phototropism) light. Shoots grow toward light; roots grow away from it. It is mediated by auxins — hormones that accumulate on the shaded side of a stem, causing cells there to elongate more. Geotropism (also called gravitropism) is growth in response to gravity: roots grow downward (positive), stems grow upward (negative). These responses help plants maximize sunlight while anchoring their roots in soil.
questions.memory_hook: Phototropism: plants grow toward light (stems) or away from it (roots). Geotropism: stems grow up, roots grow down — responding to gravity. Auxin hormones redistribute to shaded/lower sides, causing unequal elongation. Plant on a windowsill? It'll bend toward the light within days. Flip it upside down? Roots will curve back down.
